title: A Level Made of Water

pages.text:
*The Gatekeeper's Rules, Rule 6: Water in a tube cannot lie about level.*

The tube was three meters of clear plastic, salvaged from a burst irrigation line on the terraces, and it was currently full of water, trembling slightly in the morning air, and extremely difficult to keep from spilling onto Shu’s boots.

"Here," said Shu, extending one end toward her brother. "Hold this."

A-Bao took it, gripping the slick plastic with the kind of reverence usually reserved for live snakes or unexploded firecrackers, his round face set in a mask of solemn concentration. The water inside shivered, catching the sun, and a single air bubble rose to the top with the slow, arrogant dignity of a thought that does not wish to be interrupted.

"Bad," said A-Bao. "There is a liar in the water."

"There is an air bubble," said Shu. "It wants to go up. We must let it. Hold the tube high and tap it gently. Make it go."

A-Bao tapped the side of the tube with one finger. The bubble wobbled, hesitated, and then shot to the top, sticking to the ceiling of the plastic. Shu took the other end and set it on the ground. The water in the tube settled, finding its own level, a straight, unbroken line that connected the two ends despite the sag in the middle.

"Now," she said, "look at the water line on my end. It is here." She marked it with her finger. "Now look at your end. Where is it?"

A-Bao squinted. He tilted his head and moved the tube slightly, trying to see the meniscus from a different angle. "It is... higher?"

"It is the same," said Shu. "It must be the same. Water does not care if the tube is bent or twisted or tied in a knot. It only cares about gravity. Gravity pulls down. So the water stays level. Always."

A-Bao looked at the tube, then at Shu, then at the water. He picked up the tube and, in one swift motion, tied it into a severe, tight knot. The water sloshed violently, and the level line disappeared into the tangle of plastic.

"I proved it wrong," he announced, looking delighted.

"No," said Shu, untangling the knot with the patience of a woman defusing a bomb. "You proved that you cannot read a knot. Untangle it."

"I am a scientist," A-Bao said, and began to pull.
pages.image: Shu, sixteen with a black braid and indigo jacket, and A-Bao, eleven in a yellow raincoat, hold a long clear plastic tube filled with water, with A-Bao tying a knot in it, on the muddy shore of a lake.

pages.text:
They carried the tube to the edge of the Sun Basin, where the mud was still damp and glistening. Shu drove a bamboo staff into the ground on the eastern bank, marking the current water line with a sharp pencil stroke. She then walked across the exposed lakebed, the mud sucking at her boots with every step, a soft, sticky sound that made A-Bao wince from the dry side.

On the western side of the basin, near the low bank where the Moon Basin began, she drove a second staff into the ground. The water here was deep, black, and still. She held the tube against the first staff, reading the level. Then she held it against the second.

Across the whole exposed lakebed the difference was small: two centimeters of slope. The Sun Basin was flat as a table, and low, but it was not the only problem.

"Why not use a laser?" Han asked. He was sitting on a rock, his orange life vest draped over his shoulders, watching them with the bored interest of a boy who had never had to measure anything in his life. "My phone has an app. It beeps. It is very accurate."

"Your phone app," said Shu, not looking up, "has an accuracy of plus or minus ten centimeters. And it requires a battery. And it does not work when it is raining. And it does not tell you the truth about down."

"It beeps," Han said.

"I do not own a laser," Shu said, with the flat, final tone of a person who has ended a debate. "I own a tube. And a pencil. And you. Now hold the staff. Do not move. The water is trying to tell me something, and you are vibrating."

A-Bao nodded vigorously. "The water is talking. It is a shy water. It speaks in whispers."

"It is hydrostatic pressure," Shu corrected, though her voice softened. "It is simple. But it is true. And true is better than beeping."
pages.image: Shu stands in shallow, muddy water holding a bamboo staff, while Han, a tall boy in a white t-shirt and orange vest, sits on a rock watching, and A-Bao stands on the dry shore holding another staff.

pages.text:
The walk across Lantern Island was a short, steep climb over roots and stone. The island was narrow, a green spine of bamboo and camphor trees connecting the two basins, and the air smelled of wet earth and the faint, sweet rot of fallen leaves. Shu carried the tube. A-Bao carried the notebook. Han carried his dignity, which he dropped at least twice when he tripped over a root.

They reached the Moon Basin shore. The water here was high, pressing against the stone steps of the landing with a quiet, muscular insistence. Shu set the second staff in the mud at the water's edge. She held the tube against the staff in the Sun Basin, which was now a long, low, sagging line across the island.

She looked at the water level in the tube. She looked at the staff in the Sun Basin. She looked at the staff in the Moon Basin.

She did the arithmetic. She did it again. She did it a third time, because the numbers were too large to be real, too large to be a mistake.

"Three meters," she said. "And fifty centimeters."

Han whistled. It was a long, low whistle, the kind that meant *that is a lot*.

"Three and a half meters," Shu repeated, her voice tight. "The Moon Basin is three and a half meters higher than the Sun Basin. The water wants to fall that far. It wants to rush through the channel, into the east, and fill the cove. But it cannot. Something is stopping it."

She wrote it in the notebook. *HEAD = 3.5 m.* She underlined it three times. The pencil snapped against the paper, a sharp, decisive crack.

"Something is stopping it," she said again, and this time her voice was not tight. It was heavy. "What is stopping it?"
pages.image: Shu stands at the edge of the deep Moon Basin, holding a bamboo staff, looking down at the water, with A-Bao and Han standing behind her on the grassy island, the deep dark water pressing against the stone bank.

pages.text:
They sat on the grass, the notebook open between them, the tube coiled like a sleeping snake. A-Bao was eating a taro ball, the sweet, sticky mass of it disappearing in three bites, and he was looking at Shu with the eager, hungry expression of a student who knows the answer but is waiting for the teacher to ask.

"Explain," he said. "The door."

Shu wiped her hands on her trousers. "Imagine a door," she said. "A very strong one. And imagine a hand pushing against it. If the hand is weak, the door stays shut. If the hand is strong, the door opens. But the hand is not just one hand. It is the water itself. The deeper the water, the harder the push."

"But the water is just water," A-Bao said.

"Yes. But it is a lot of water," Shu replied. "And it is three and a half meters deep. The pressure at the bottom is... let us see." She pulled out her calculator. "Density of water is one thousand kilograms per cubic meter. Gravity is nine point eight. Depth is three point five meters. Multiply them. One thousand, times nine point eight, times three point five."

She typed it in. She looked at the number. She typed it in again.

"Thirty-four thousand three hundred," she said. "Pascals."

"That is a lot of Pascals," A-Bao said.

"It is a lot of force," Shu corrected. "If the gate is one square meter, that is thirty-four thousand newtons. That is... that is about three and a half tonnes of force. Pushing against the gate. Every second. Every minute. For thirty years."

A-Bao dropped his taro ball. It rolled off the grass and vanished into the ferns. He did not chase it. He was looking at Shu with a new, serious respect.

"The gate is holding back three and a half tonnes," he said. "Every second."

"Yes," said Shu. "And if it breaks, the water will not ask permission. It will just go."
pages.image: Shu sits on the grass with a calculator in her hand, looking concerned, while A-Bao sits beside her holding a taro ball, and Han leans against a tree, the deep Moon Basin water visible in the background.

pages.text:
The sun was lowering, turning the mist on the far shore into a soft, golden haze. On the opposite bank, the survey team from the Taihe Power Company moved with the brisk, purposeful energy of people who had a schedule, a cluster of white shirts and yellow hard hats crossing the water. Ouyang Min walked toward them, her white sneakers splashing through the shallow current while she kept her roll of plans tucked firmly under her arm.

She stopped at the edge of the mud. Her gaze traveled over the clear plastic tube coiled on the grass, then drifted to the two bamboo staffs driven deep into the earth at opposite ends of the basin. Finally, her eyes settled on Shu, who sat with her notebook resting in her lap.

"That is a better level than the one my people brought," Ouyang said. Her voice was calm, precise, and entirely devoid of irony.

Shu blinked. "It is a tube."

"It is a level," Ouyang corrected. "And it is accurate. Furthermore, it does not require a battery. Show me the numbers."

Shu hesitated. The notebook was hers, and the measurements within it were hers, but the truth of the lake belonged to everyone. She glanced at A-Bao, who was nodding vigorously, and then at Han, who offered a shrug so vague and helpful it might as well have been a question mark drawn in the air.

Shu opened the notebook and turned to the page with the three heavy underlines. She held it out.

Ouyang took it. She read the numbers, then read them again, her lips moving silently as she calculated. She pulled out her own small, crisp notebook and scribbled a quick, sharp note. When she looked up, her expression was unreadable.

"Three point five meters," Ouyang said. "That is a significant head. Your gates are under immense stress. If they are old, they are likely to fail."

"They are not old," Shu said. "They are jammed."

Ouyang looked at her. She did not smile, nor did she frown. She simply looked at the water, at the deep, dark, pressing surface of the Moon Basin, and then back to Shu.

"Jammed," Ouyang repeated. "Then the water is still pushing. And the time is still running."
pages.image: Ouyang Min, a tall woman with a yellow hard hat and white shirt, stands in the shallow water holding a notebook, looking at Shu who sits on the grass, with the deep Moon Basin water and the misty far shore in the background.
